text.p: Companies increasingly are leaving the details of flextime arrangements up to supervisors to work out with their employees.
Several businesses polled said they have no formal policies but adopt flexible work schedules as needed.

Reasons given include easing traffic congestion at manufacturing plants; staffing desks around the clock to satisfy calls from global customers; getting maximum use from equipment; and as a way to boost employee morale.
"There are certainly any number of cases where employees come in early and leave early or work late and leave late," said Don Herring, public affairs manager at USX Corp.
The Pittsburgh employer of 42,000 has no formal flextime policy. "It's kind of left up to department discretion," Herring said.
Motorola Inc. spokeswoman Margo Brown said, "It's up to the manager. We say, 'If it works within the needs of your business, you can pretty much do whatever you want.'"
Kathy Zweber, the company's director for work/life and wellness, who has just put the finishing touches on her book, "Flexible Work Options"(Motorola University Press), said:

"We do approximately 65 percent of our business outside the United States. So when you're dealing with customers on the other side of the world it's a benefit to have people working other than 8 to 5 in the U.S.

"We view them (flextime arrangements) as something that gives the company a business advantage. We run our manufacturing operations 24 hours a day seven days a week, so having our employees working on different schedules is not a deterrant to doing business."

Speaking personally, Zweber said, "I work around my (five) children's schedule and business needs. When I come back from a business trip I spend more time at home, and occasionally work from home." And she makes a point of going home two afternoons a week "at the same time that school gets out."
Seattle-based Boeing Co. finds flextime helps with "24-hour manning of phones" to satisfy requests by airline customers for spare parts, spokesman Peter Conte said.
Boeing has no formal flextime policy, but Conte said, "if it's a hardship to be at work at 7:30 a.m. and work until 4, but easier to work from 8 to 4:30, that accommodation is made."

To "alleviate the crush of people arriving or leaving" at its 30,000-employee Everett, Wash., plant, Boeing staggers the time employees arrive for the morning shift at 20-minute intervals starting at 5:40 a.m., Conte said.
Union Electric of St. Louis, an employer of 6,000, has had flextime for nine years, according to Ray Steinnerd, supervisor of compensation.
"Better coverage" for customers was one reason for allowing employees to elect to start as early as 6:30 a.m., and "running equipment longer during the day, like in the computer area," was another.
"Some people said that if they could work earlier in the morning when other people weren't around, they could get more work done due to fewer interruptions," Steinnerd added.
"The downside," he noted, "is that employees are not always available when you need them. You can't schedule a meeting early in the morning or late in the afternoon."
So United Electric established "core hours" between 9 a.m. and 3 p.m. "when we knew everyone would be here," Steinnerd said.
